clinicalPearls: The porphyrias are metabolic disorders, each from deficient (or, for XLP, increased) activity of a specific enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway; inherited as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked, except porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) which is usually sporadic (p.3340).
Classified as hepatic or erythropoietic (by primary site of porphyrin/precursor overproduction) and as acute or cutaneous (by clinical manifestation) (p.3340, 3344).
Acute hepatic porphyrias (AIP, HCP, VP) usually present in adult life after puberty with acute attacks of neurovisceral symptoms and elevated urinary porphyrin precursors ALA and/or PBG (p.3344).

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is autosomal dominant from half-normal HMB-synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase) activity; the most common acute hepatic porphyria (~1 in 20,000 Caucasians), especially frequent in Scandinavia and Great Britain (p.3340, 3346).
AIP abdominal pain is the most common symptom: poorly localized, often with cramping, ileus, distention, and decreased bowel sounds (though increased bowel sounds and diarrhea may occur) (p.3346).

AIP attacks also feature nausea, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia, hypertension, mental symptoms, limb/head/neck/chest pain, muscle weakness, sensory loss, dysuria, and urinary retention; tachycardia, hypertension, restlessness, tremor, and sweating reflect sympathetic overactivity (p.3346).

AIP peripheral neuropathy is due to axonal degeneration (not demyelination) and primarily affects motor neurons; proximal muscles (shoulders/arms) are involved first, and it may be focal or involve cranial nerves (p.3346).
Mental symptoms in acute attacks include anxiety, insomnia, depression, disorientation, hallucinations, and paranoia; seizures may be neurologic or due to hyponatremia (p.3346).

Diagnosis of an acute attack rests on substantial elevation of urinary PBG (and ALA); urinary PBG is always increased during acute attacks of AIP, HCP, and VP and is not substantially raised in any other condition, making a spot urine PBG both sensitive and specific (p.3345-3346).
PCT is the most common porphyria overall; hepatic URO-decarboxylase is deficient in all types, and ~80% of patients have no UROD mutation (sporadic type 1) (p.3347).

PCT presents with blistering, photosensitive skin lesions most commonly on the backs of the hands that rupture, crust, and scar, with skin friability, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation; neurologic features are absent (p.3347).

An acute attack may begin with sharp abdominal pain, then agitation/hallucinations/seizures, with back and extremity pain followed by weakness several days later, mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome; weakness may be asymmetric, proximal or distal, and involve facial/bulbar muscles (p.3602-3603).
Urine may appear brownish during an attack due to high porphyrin metabolite concentration (p.3602-3603).
harrison.pathophysiology: Each porphyria results from deficient (or, in XLP, increased) activity of one of the eight enzymes of the heme biosynthetic pathway converting glycine and succinyl-CoA to heme. In acute hepatic porphyrias, half-normal enzyme activity becomes limiting when hepatic heme synthesis is increased: induction of the rate-limiting hepatic gene ALAS1 (regulated in part by PGC-1alpha, which is induced by fasting) leads to accumulation and urinary excretion of the porphyrin precursors ALA and PBG, which underlie the acute neurovisceral attacks. Common precipitating factors include endogenous and exogenous steroids (estrogens/progestins), porphyrinogenic drugs (often P450-metabolized), alcohol, low-calorie/low-carbohydrate diets, infections, and surgery. AIP is almost always latent before puberty, suggesting adult steroid hormone levels drive expression; symptoms are commoner in women, with premenstrual (luteal-phase progesterone) attacks. Hyponatremia results from hypothalamic involvement with inappropriate vasopressin secretion or from electrolyte depletion (vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, renal sodium loss). In PCT, substantial deficiency of hepatic URO-decarboxylase (to ~20% of normal or less, via an iron- and oxidative-stress-dependent uroporphomethene inhibitor) causes accumulation of porphyrins that, on excitation by long-wave UV light in the skin, produce blistering photosensitivity (p.3340, 3345-3347).
additionalDifferentials: Intestinal obstruction (acute abdomen) - pain of porphyria is usually difficult to distinguish because severe hyperperistalsis is prominent in both (p.3344-ch.40)
Lead colic / lead intoxication (lead inhibits ALA-dehydratase, raising urinary ALA and coproporphyrin III) (p.3342, ch.40)
Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (succinylacetone inhibits ALA-dehydratase, mimicking acute porphyria) (p.3342)
Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute attack with ascending weakness mimics GBS) (p.3603)
Chronic liver disease (can cause nonspecific increases in urinary porphyrins leading to misdiagnosis) (p.3345)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute surgical abdomen / intestinal obstruction (acute hepatic porphyria attack mimics this) (p.3344, ch.40)
Lead poisoning (lead colic and neuropathy mimic acute porphyria) (p.3342)
Guillain-Barre syndrome (ascending motor weakness in an acute attack) (p.3603)
Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (biochemical and clinical mimic of acute porphyria) (p.3342)
additionalInvestigations: Spot (single-void) urine for porphobilinogen (PBG) - first-line; always raised in acute attacks of AIP/HCP/VP and specific; 24-h collection unnecessary (p.3345-3346)
Quantitative urinary ALA, PBG, and creatinine on the same spot sample (also detects ADP) (p.3345)
Total urinary porphyrins (interpret cautiously - often nonspecific) (p.3345)
Urinary, fecal, and plasma porphyrins to distinguish AIP from HCP and VP (fecal porphyrins normal/minimal in AIP) (p.3346)
Total plasma porphyrins with fluorometric scanning of diluted plasma at neutral pH (distinguishes VP from PCT; VP emission peak ~626 nm) for cutaneous porphyrias (p.3346, 3348)
Erythrocyte protoporphyrin (more sensitive for EPP/XLP; confirm EPP by predominant free, not zinc, protoporphyrin) (p.3346)
Isocoproporphyrins in feces - diagnostic of hepatic URO-decarboxylase deficiency (PCT) (p.3348)
Erythrocyte URO-decarboxylase activity (~50% in type 2 PCT; markedly deficient, 3-10%, in HEP) (p.3348)
Molecular genetic mutation analysis of the relevant heme-pathway gene (definitive; diagnostic even when precursor levels have normalized, and for latent heterozygotes/relatives) (p.3342, 3346)
redFlags: Acute neurovisceral attack: severe poorly-localized abdominal pain with autonomic instability (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating), motor neuropathy/weakness, and psychiatric disturbance - the AIP acute hepatic porphyria red-flag constellation (p.3346)
Hyponatremia (from inappropriate vasopressin secretion or electrolyte depletion) and seizures during an attack (p.3346)
Markedly raised urinary PBG/ALA in a patient with abdominal pain after puberty (p.3345-3346)
Exposure to a porphyria-precipitating drug, low-calorie diet, alcohol, infection, or surgery preceding the attack (p.3346)
Progression to respiratory and bulbar paralysis; sudden death may result from sympathetic overactivity and cardiac arrhythmia, especially with delayed diagnosis/treatment (p.3346)
harrison.prognosis: AIP can be disabling but is rarely fatal; the prognosis of individuals with HMBS mutations is generally favorable, and most heterozygotes remain latent. When an attack resolves, abdominal pain may disappear within hours and paresis begins to improve within days, sometimes continuing to improve over years; recovery from severe motor neuropathy may take months to years and depends on the degree of neuronal damage and early treatment. Long-term complications of AIP include increased risk of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (up to 59% develop CKD), chronic liver function abnormalities with increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (warranting hepatic imaging at least every 6 months), and persistent neuropathy, fatigue, chronic pain, nausea, depression, and anxiety. Homozygous dominant AIP usually presents in infancy and most affected children die at an early age. PCT can almost always be brought into complete remission with treatment, but patients characteristically have chronic liver disease, sometimes cirrhosis, and are at risk for hepatocellular carcinoma (p.3346-3348).
pitfalls: A great mimic of the acute abdomen: porphyric (and lead colic) pain is hard to distinguish from intestinal obstruction because of prominent hyperperistalsis - risking unnecessary surgery (p.3344, ch.40).
Because symptoms are nonspecific and rarely occur before puberty, diagnosis is often delayed; a high index of suspicion is required (p.3340, 3346).
Measuring urinary porphyrins alone for screening should be avoided - minimal nonspecific increases (e.g., in chronic liver disease) cause misdiagnosis; use urinary PBG (p.3345).

Erythrocyte HMB-synthase assay is not a useful first-line test: activity is not decreased in all AIP patients, borderline-low values are not diagnostic, and it is not deficient in other acute porphyrias; some HMBS mutations give normal erythrocyte enzyme so genetic testing is needed (p.3345-3346).
ALA/PBG levels often remain high after symptoms resolve, so diagnosing an acute attack in a biochemically proven AIP patient relies primarily on clinical features (p.3346).
Most antiseizure drugs can exacerbate AIP, making seizure treatment difficult (clonazepam may be safer than phenytoin or barbiturates) (p.3346).
Abdominal tenderness, fever, and leukocytosis are usually absent or mild in AIP because the process is neurologic, not inflammatory - their prominence should prompt reconsideration (p.3346).
In PCT, neurologic features are absent - abdominal/neurovisceral attacks should not be attributed to it (p.3347).
harrison.severityClassification: Porphyrias are classified by primary overproduction site (hepatic vs erythropoietic) and by clinical manifestation (acute neurovisceral vs cutaneous). Acute hepatic porphyrias: AIP, HCP, VP (and the rare autosomal recessive ADP) present with acute neurovisceral attacks and raised ALA/PBG; AIP causes neurovisceral disease without photosensitivity, whereas HCP and VP can have both neurovisceral attacks and PCT-like cutaneous photosensitivity. Cutaneous: PCT (and HEP) present with chronic blistering photosensitivity. Erythropoietic porphyrias (CEP, EPP, XLP) present with cutaneous photosensitivity (EPP/XLP non-blistering, immediate and painful). Acute-attack severity ranges from mild (abdominal pain without paresis or hyponatremia, manageable with carbohydrate loading) to severe (paresis, hyponatremia, bulbar/respiratory paralysis) (p.3340, 3344, 3346-3347).
